clue.text: Patriotic work of Du Maurier

parts.note: the clue reads as a stirring flag-waving song, but it is also the title of Daphne du Maurier's last novel, which borrows that song's name

explanation.surface: A question about which of Daphne du Maurier's books shows the most love of country.
explanation.walkthrough: Daphne du Maurier's 1972 novel shares its title with the 18th-century British patriotic song, so one title answers both readings.
explanation.definitionFit: The song is a famous British patriotic anthem and the same title was given to a du Maurier novel.

clue.text: Wiggin's girl, a thing of fire and spirit

definitions.text: Wiggin's girl, a thing of fire and spirit

parts.words: Wiggin's girl, a thing of fire and spirit
parts.note: Kate Douglas Wiggin's heroine of Sunnybrook Farm is described in the novel in just these words, so the clue asks for her full name

explanation.surface: A character sketch of a spirited girl from a Kate Douglas Wiggin novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Kate Douglas Wiggin wrote Rebecca of Sunnybrook Farm; its heroine's full name is Rebecca Rowena Randall, and the book calls her 'a thing of fire and spirit'.
explanation.definitionFit: The heroine of Wiggin's Sunnybrook Farm novel bears this name and is described in the book with the quoted phrase.

clue.text: A quarter of Harland

parts.note: Henry Harland's novel A ...-Quarter Courtship is set in the Paris district of students and artists, so the quarter is named for that book

explanation.surface: Seems to ask for one fourth of the name Harland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A quarter' looks like a fraction of the word Harland, but it is a city district: Henry Harland wrote A Latin-Quarter Courtship, set in the student district of Paris.
explanation.definitionFit: The Left Bank district of Paris is called by this name, and Harland titled a novel after it.

clue.text: His Crusoe was found on the western prairies

definitions.text: His Crusoe was found on the western prairies

parts.words: His Crusoe was found on the western prairies
parts.note: the Crusoe here is not Defoe's castaway but a dog, hero of a Victorian boys' story subtitled A Tale of the Western Prairies

explanation.surface: Suggests a Robinson Crusoe story moved from a desert island to the American plains.
explanation.walkthrough: R. M. Ballantyne wrote The Dog Crusoe: A Tale of the Western Prairies (1861); the clue hopes the solver thinks of Defoe first.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scottish author R. M. Ballantyne wrote The Dog Crusoe, subtitled A Tale of the Western Prairies.

clue.text: Appearing in The Caliph, it used to be thought he was slain by Hercules Somehow muted as unlucky Argonaut, also. Dies young, wife dying to restore him

indicators.note: the answer is appearing in, that is sitting inside, the run of letters spanning these clue words

explanation.surface: A tale from the Arabian Nights crossed with Greek myth about a victim of Hercules.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'CaliPH, IT USed'. The newspaper text runs on with 5-down's clue, which belongs to that light only.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Iphitus, son of Eurytus, was thrown from the walls of Tiryns by Heracles in a fit of madness.

clue.text: Somehow muted as unlucky Argonaut, also. Dies young, wife dying to restore him

definitions.text: unlucky Argonaut, also. Dies young, wife dying to restore him

indicators.note: somehow means in some way or other, telling the solver to rearrange the two words that follow

explanation.surface: A mythic tale of a doomed sailor whose wife gives up her life for his.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Somehow' rearranges MUTED AS. Admetus sailed with the Argonauts; fated to die young, he was saved when his wife Alcestis agreed to die in his place.
explanation.definitionFit: King Admetus of Pherae, an Argonaut, was spared early death when his wife Alcestis took his place among the dead.

clue.text: Bad omen for Verne's Indian prince

indicators.note: bad here means spoilt or out of order, so the letters of the next word are jumbled

explanation.surface: An ill omen hanging over a character in a Jules Verne novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bad' rearranges OMEN. Captain Nemo of Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea is revealed in The Mysterious Island to be the Indian Prince Dakkar.
explanation.definitionFit: Verne's submarine captain is disclosed as the Indian prince Dakkar, so the prince's adopted name fits.

clue.text: … the bay/ From whence at first she weigh'd her 7 (Titus Andronicus)

definitions.text: the bay/ From whence at first she weigh'd her 7 (Titus Andronicus)

parts.words: the bay/ From whence at first she weigh'd her 7 (Titus Andronicus)
parts.note: a fill-in quotation from Shakespeare's play, the 7 standing for the missing word; the ship returns to the place where she was moored

explanation.surface: A line from Titus Andronicus about a ship sailing home to harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: In Act 1 Scene 1, Titus returns to Rome 'as the bark that hath discharged her fraught / Returns with precious lading to the bay / From whence at first she weigh'd her anchorage'.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship's mooring place is the spot where she lay at anchor, which fills the gap in Shakespeare's line.

clue.text: Green's forgetful ones?

parts.note: Gerald Green wrote a novel about expatriates in Ceylon, named after the people of Homer's Odyssey whose fruit made them forget home

explanation.surface: Asks what an author named Green called people who keep forgetting things.
explanation.walkthrough: Gerald Green's 1959 novel shares its title with Tennyson's poem; in the Odyssey, eating the lotus fruit makes Odysseus's men forget their homecoming.
explanation.definitionFit: The lotus-eaters of Homer lose all memory of home, so forgetful people are named after them, as is Green's novel.

clue.text: Palestinian objective lazily approached by Yeats's rough beast

definitions.text: Palestinian objective lazily approached by Yeats's rough beast

parts.words: Palestinian objective lazily approached by Yeats's rough beast
parts.note: Yeats's poem The Second Coming ends with a rough beast that 'slouches' towards a town in Palestine to be born

explanation.surface: A political-sounding sentence about a Palestinian goal approached by a lumbering creature.
explanation.walkthrough: The last lines of Yeats's The Second Coming: 'And what rough beast, its hour come round at last, / Slouches towards Bethlehem to be born?' 'Lazily approached' paraphrases 'slouches towards'.
explanation.definitionFit: The town of the Nativity lies in Palestine and is the destination of the beast in Yeats's poem.

clue.text: Mich, a mistaken prophet

indicators.note: mistaken means wrong, so the letters of the preceding words are put in a different order

explanation.surface: Someone called Mich has wrongly set themselves up as a seer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mistaken' rearranges MICHA, from 'Mich, a'.
explanation.definitionFit: Micah is one of the minor prophets of the Hebrew Bible, with a book named after him.

clue.text: Roman poet sounds like a transgressor

indicators.note: sounds like tells the solver the answer is said the same way as a word for the following phrase

parts.note: a transgressor is a person who sins, a sinner

explanation.surface: A remark that a Latin poet's name has an unfortunate ring to it.
explanation.walkthrough: Gaius Helvius Cinna was a Roman poet, the one torn apart by the mob in Julius Caesar because he shared a conspirator's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Helvius Cinna wrote neoteric verse in the late Roman Republic, a friend of Catullus.

clue.text: Réalisateur is tawdry stuff, I see

parts.note: tat is cheap, tasteless goods, tawdry stuff

explanation.surface: A French film director dismissed as trash, as if the speaker sees through him.
explanation.walkthrough: Réalisateur is French for film director; Jacques Tati made Monsieur Hulot's Holiday. 'is' and 'see' join the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Jacques Tati was a French film director, which is what the French word réalisateur names.

clue.text: Kavanagh's was on the market

parts.note: Patrick Kavanagh titled a 1947 poetry collection with a phrase saying his inner self was up for sale

explanation.surface: Suggests that something belonging to a man called Kavanagh was being sold.
explanation.walkthrough: The Irish poet Patrick Kavanagh published Soul for Sale in 1947.
explanation.definitionFit: Kavanagh's collection Soul for Sale offers the poet's spirit for purchase in its title.

clue.text: Madrigalist may be first foreigner to go wrong over a second-rate large firm

indicators.note: over in a down clue means the earlier pieces sit above the later ones
first picks only the opening letter of the word it qualifies

parts.note: to err is to go wrong
B is the second grade, so second-rate
OS is the clothing abbreviation for outsize, large
CO is the abbreviation for company, a firm

explanation.surface: A tale of a foreign singer whose career collapses over a big but shoddy business.
explanation.walkthrough: Alfonso Ferrabosco was an Italian composer of madrigals who worked at the Elizabethan court.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfonso Ferrabosco the elder wrote madrigals that helped bring the Italian form to England.

clue.text: Argonaut producing dramatis personae (American)

parts.note: dramatis personae are the characters of a play, a cast

explanation.surface: A Greek hero who comes up with a full cast list for a play from the States.
explanation.walkthrough: Acastus, son of Pelias, joined Jason's Argonauts against his father's wishes.
explanation.definitionFit: Acastus, son of King Pelias of Iolcus, sailed on the Argo with Jason.

clue.text: Yeti starting to upset somebody. A churlish Shakespearian philosopher

parts.note: a yeti is an ape-man of the Himalayas

indicators.note: starting picks the opening letter of each of the three words that follow it

explanation.surface: An abominable snowman setting out to annoy someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'starting' takes the first letters of 'to upset somebody', giving TUS. Apemantus is the cynic of Timon of Athens.
explanation.definitionFit: In Timon of Athens the surly cynic who rails at Timon's flatterers is called Apemantus.

clue.text: Brothel painting from Michael Innes?

parts.note: a stew is an old word for a brothel
painting is a form of art

explanation.surface: Asks for a picture of a bawdy house by a detective novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: Michael Innes was the pen name of J. I. M. Stewart, who wrote academic novels under his own name and detective fiction under the pseudonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Michael Innes was the pseudonym of the Oxford don J. I. M. Stewart, so the surname is behind the name.

clue.text: Average navy unserviceable at the gateway to hell

parts.note: ave. is an abbreviation for average
RN is the Royal Navy

explanation.surface: A run-of-the-mill fleet sits useless at the mouth of the underworld.
explanation.walkthrough: Lake Avernus near Naples was thought by the Romans to be the entrance to the underworld.
explanation.definitionFit: The crater lake near Cumae was held in Roman myth to be the way down to the realm of the dead.

clue.text: Mosaic spy. Or Davidson, so to speak

explanation.surface: A pseudonymous agent under Moses, or a man called Davidson.
explanation.walkthrough: In Numbers 13 Moses sends twelve spies into Canaan, one being Shammua son of Zaccur; 2 Samuel 5 lists a different Shammua as a son born to David in Jerusalem.
explanation.definitionFit: One biblical Shammua spied out Canaan for Moses; another was literally David's son, written as one word.

clue.text: Novelist as member of privileged class

explanation.surface: A writer described as one of the elite.
explanation.walkthrough: Anthony Burgess wrote A Clockwork Orange; a burgess was a freeman of a borough with civic privileges.
explanation.definitionFit: Anthony Burgess was an English writer of fiction; a burgess was a citizen holding the franchise of a borough.

clue.text: Lady Jones. Possibly dine with her

definitions.text: Lady Jones. Possibly dine with her

parts.words: Lady Jones. Possibly dine with her
parts.note: the novelist was Lady Jones by marriage; her first name is a rearrangement of the word dine, and goes with the surname asked for

explanation.surface: An invitation to have dinner with a titled lady.
explanation.walkthrough: Enid Bagnold, author of National Velvet, married Sir Roderick Jones. 'Possibly dine' gives ENID, which goes 'with' the surname.
explanation.definitionFit: The author of National Velvet became Lady Jones on marrying Sir Roderick Jones of Reuters.

clue.text: Expensive ego of Ustinov?

explanation.surface: Asks whether Peter Ustinov's self-regard came at a high price.
explanation.walkthrough: Peter Ustinov's autobiography is Dear Me, so the word paired with 'me' (ego) in his title is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: Costly things are said to be this; Ustinov titled his memoir with this word before 'Me'.

clue.text: White dog in London

parts.note: the dog is not in the city but in a novel by Jack London, the wolfdog of the Yukon

explanation.surface: Looks like a pale dog loose on the streets of the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'London' is Jack London, whose novel White Fang follows a wolfdog in the Yukon.
explanation.definitionFit: Jack London's wolfdog hero is called White Fang, so the second half of the name is wanted.

clue.text: Provenance of Orwell's days

parts.note: Orwell's first novel is named for the days spent in the colony where he served in the police

explanation.surface: Asks where Orwell's days came from.
explanation.walkthrough: George Orwell's novel Burmese Days (1934) draws on his years in the Indian Imperial Police there.
explanation.definitionFit: Orwell's novel Burmese Days is set in the country where he served as a colonial policeman.

clue.text: Island goddess

explanation.surface: A goddess with an island to her name.
explanation.walkthrough: Rhode Island is the smallest US state; Rhode (Rhodos) was a sea nymph, wife of Helios, after whom Rhodes is named.
explanation.definitionFit: The word begins the name Rhode Island, and in Greek myth Rhode was a sea goddess, consort of the sun god Helios.

clue.text: Mason's cleric associated with 20D's country gentleman

definitions.text: Mason's cleric associated with 20D's country gentleman

parts.words: Mason's cleric associated with 20D's country gentleman
parts.note: A. E. W. Mason wrote a novel about a senior clergyman's elbow, and Bagnold wrote one about a squire

explanation.surface: A churchman linked with a landowner, from two authors' books.
explanation.walkthrough: A. E. W. Mason wrote The Dean's Elbow (1930); 20D, Enid Bagnold, wrote The Squire (1938), and the dean and squire are the two village dignitaries.
explanation.definitionFit: A dean is the senior cleric of a cathedral chapter, and gives the title of Mason's novel The Dean's Elbow.

clue.text: Forgotten the name of this river?

definitions.text: Forgotten the name of this river?

parts.words: Forgotten the name of this river?
parts.note: the river of the classical underworld whose waters make the dead forget, so forgetting its name fits it

explanation.surface: A quizmaster asks if you have forgotten which river this is.
explanation.walkthrough: In Greek myth the dead drink from this river of the underworld to forget their earthly lives.
explanation.definitionFit: The underworld river of oblivion in Greek myth wipes the memory of those who drink it.

clue.text: Sort of note on satellites by Collins

indicators.note: on in an across clue puts the first piece after the second

parts.note: moons are natural satellites of planets
a tone is a kind of musical note

explanation.surface: A musical description of a sound placed on top of satellites, credited to someone named Collins.
explanation.walkthrough: Wilkie Collins wrote The Moonstone (1868), often called the first English detective novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Wilkie Collins's 1868 detective novel is titled The Moonstone.

clue.text: Lawrence characters not quite dons nor slaves

indicators.note: not quite means not exactly, so the letters of the following words are not in the right order

explanation.surface: Lawrence's characters are neither academics nor servants.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not quite' rearranges DONS NOR SLAVES. D. H. Lawrence's novel Sons and Lovers follows Paul Morel, his mother and his lovers.
explanation.definitionFit: The title of D. H. Lawrence's novel describes its people: Paul Morel and his brothers, and the women he loves.
